BaseText-eqOrNE About-dhJljB deqABF gCnmYV hUFKXn"><div data-testid="AboutDescription">University of Cambridge Research Fellow Dr. Stephen Turton joins WIRED to answer the internet's burning questions about the logic (and many quirks) of the English language. Why are so many English words not pronounced the way they're spelled? Why is the plural of 'child' not 'childs' but 'children?' 'Foot' becomes 'feet' but 'boot' does't pluralize to 'beet?' How do we know what Old English sounded like? Why is the letter R pronounced so different across languages? What does a pineapple have to do with either pines OR apples? Answers to these questions and many more await on Etymology Support.

class="BaseWrap-sc-gzmcOU BaseText-eqOrNE TranscriptSectionWrapper-vgIuE deqABF fFOlvo jlCFLn"><p data-testid="transcript-caption-0">Hi, I&#x27;m Stephen Turton, and this is Etymology Support.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-1">[upbeat music]</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-2">First question.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-3">SamuelM80056720 asks,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-4">I have a semi-serious question for etymologists.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-5">If feet is the plural for foot,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-6">why is beet not the plural of boot?</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-7">Is it because of the vegetable?</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-8">Foot belongs to a category of words</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-9">that derive from Old English in which to make the plural,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-10">you change the vowel in the word.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-11">So other words in this category</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-12">are tooth-teeth, and goose-geese, mouse-mice.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-13">Book also used to be in this category in Old English,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-14">but later on we regularized the spelling,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-15">so it&#x27;s book-books.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-16">If we&#x27;d kept the Old English pattern,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-17">it would now be one book, two beech.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-18">The word boot, on the other hand, is not from Old English.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-19">It was borrowed from French into Middle English,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-20">which is why it just gets the default plural -s.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-21">There are lots of different ways of pluralizing nouns</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-22">in Old English.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-23">So you might form the plural</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-24">by changing the vowel in the base word,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-25">or you might form the plural by adding a suffix,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-26">which could be, -as, -a, -an, -u, -ru.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-27">In the Middle English period most of these ways</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-28">of forming the plural fell out of use</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-29">and the -s plural came to predominate.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-30">So it basically replaced the old plurals</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-31">for a lot of English words just because it was easier.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-32">SharPhoe asks, Weird etymology question.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-33">When and why did whoops/oops</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-34">become the default sound made when making a mistake?</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-35">So, whoops is actually more recent than you might think.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-36">The earliest evidence we have of whoops being used</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-37">in writing dates to the 19th century.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-38">It actually seems to have been derived from oops-a-daisy,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-39">which we have slightly earlier evidence for.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-40">Oops-a-daisy might have been</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-41">a kind of whimsical alteration of lackadaisy,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-42">which is in turn a whimsical alteration of alack-a-day,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-43">which is in turn a whimsical alteration of alack,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-44">which is a very old way of saying, oh no.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-45">This is from the FindingFennsGold subreddit.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-46">Origin of the word clue.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-47">Clue originally meant a ball of thread.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-48">Then, during Middle English it came to be associated</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-49">with the Greek myth of Theseus</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-50">who used a ball of thread to find his way in and out</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-51">of the Minotaur&#x27;s Labyrinth by unspooling it on the way in</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-52">and then following it back out.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-53">From this, a clue came to mean</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-54">something that helped lead you to a solution to a problem.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-55">And that is now the only meaning</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-56">which is common in English today.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-57">RonilBBK asks, Silent letters in words</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-58">don&#x27;t make any sense.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-59">How about you just don&#x27;t add the letter in the word?</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-60">So there are a couple of reasons</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-61">that silent letters exist in English.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-62">One is that the pronunciation of the language has changed</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-63">and the spelling system just hasn&#x27;t kept up with it.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-64">For example, the G-H in words</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-65">like through and thought and night.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-66">The G-H exists there</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-67">because that sound used to be pronounced.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-68">In Old English and Middle English,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-69">that was the velar fricative [vocalizes].</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-70">Eventually, because that&#x27;s quite a difficult sound</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-71">to pronounce, it dropped out of the language,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-72">but we continue to spell words with that G-H</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-73">through a process of sheer inertia.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-74">There have been calls for spelling reform in English</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-75">for literally centuries.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-76">In the 19th century, one author complained</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-77">that the word fish might as well be spelled G-H-O-T-I.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-78">G-H, as in the f at the end of rough,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-79">O as in the i in women,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-80">and T-I as in the sh in mention.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-81">Now, in reality no would actually spell fish this way</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-82">because we know that there are implicit rules</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-83">to where letter combinations can go in words.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-84">So we know that G-H can stand for the sound f,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-85">but only at the end of a word, as in rough, enough, tough.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-86">There was also a moment in time where a word like mention</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-87">would&#x27;ve been pronounced ment-i-on or something like that.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-88">But the T-I-O-N in English,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-89">if you say it enough times over and over,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-90">tion, ti-an, ti-an, chi-an, chi-an, chin, shin,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-91">it just becomes a lot easier to say shin.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-92">So T-I I becomes sh.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-93">Ease of articulation is a common trigger</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-94">for sound change in English and other languages.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-95">Crowzur asks, Why do question words,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-96">why, who, where, when, et cetera, all start with WW-H?</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-97">So this goes all the way back to Proto-Indo-European,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-98">which is the earliest ancestor of the English language</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-99">and many other European and Asian languages</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-100">that etymologists have been able to reconstruct.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-101">Proto-Indo-European had an interrogative stem,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-102">an element of a word that would go into building other words</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-103">that looked something like qui.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-104">And this and its variants were used to coin question words,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-105">And this qui survives into many modern languages.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-106">So for example, in French and Spanish as Q-U</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-107">as in qui, que, quando, quel.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-108">It also survives in English as W-H.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-109">And the resemblance is easy to see</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-110">once you know that the original spelling</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-111">and pronunciation in English was H-W, hua.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-112">Nobody ever actually said wa-ha.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-113">If you listen to older speakers today</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-114">who still pronounce the H in these question words,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-115">you will hear that they put the H before the W.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-116">So it&#x27;s what, why, when.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-117">At jpk_murphy asks,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-118">Wonder where the word salary originated.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-119">So the word salary comes from Latin salarium,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-120">which ultimately comes from sal meaning salt.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-121">In ancient Rome, a salarium was a wage paid to somebody</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-122">so that they could buy salt and other household goods.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-123">The word salad ultimately derives from the same root, sal,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-124">because a salad was a cold dish that was seasoned with salt.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-125">This comes from the etymology subreddit.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-126">What&#x27;s going on with the word child?</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-127">Why does it pluralize into children rather than childs?</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-128">Child goes all the way back to Old English,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-129">which had multiple methods of forming a plural.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-130">One of the plurals for the word child in Old English</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-131">was childru.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-132">During Middle English, this became childre.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-133">However, at a later second plural ending N,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-136">as in ox-oxen, to create the word children.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-137">So it actually has two plural endings</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-138">stacked on top of each other.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-139">It&#x27;s equivalent to saying childses.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-140">Delarosajl24 asks, Why do we call it deadline</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-141">for when something is due?</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-142">What does death have to do with finishing projects on time?</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-143">So this is a bit of a grizzly story.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-144">During the American Civil War,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-145">a deadline was a literal boundary around a prison</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-146">that prisoners were not allowed to cross</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-147">without being in danger of being shot.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-148">From that, a deadline came to be used metaphorically</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-149">to mean a point of no return.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-150">And that&#x27;s why we get the sense of a date</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-151">on which something is due.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-152">Jbud3570 asks,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-153">Why are there multiple words that mean the same thing?</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-154">There are actually very few true synonyms</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-155">in English or in other languages.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-156">You know words that have exactly the same meaning</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-157">in all contexts.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-158">Even if two words appear to have exactly the same meaning,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-159">they will tend to be used in somewhat different contexts.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-160">For contexts,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-167">but we prefer to use the word large</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-168">only with its literal meaning.</p><p in English we have the words</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-172">kingly, royal, and regal.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-173">They all mean the same thing,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-176">and regal comes from Latin rex, also meaning king.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-177">Dworkphone asks, Is there any reason</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-180">The word alphabet comes from alpha beta,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-181">which are the first two letters of the Greek alphabet,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-182">and they correspond to Latin A and B.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-183">Exactly how the letters ended up in this order,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-184">A, B, C, or alpha, beta, gamma,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-185">or ah, ba, ca, or ah, ba, ga is not known.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-186">It might have been random to an extent,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-187">but it&#x27;s also worth noting that a lot of these sounds</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-188">are the first sounds that human babies make</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-189">when they first start babbling,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-190">a, a, ba, ba, ga, ga, ca, ca, da, da.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-191">The Latin alphabet ultimately derives</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-192">from the Greek alphabet,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-193">which in turn ultimately derives</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-194">from the Phoenician alphabet.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-195">And in all of these alphabets,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-196">the letter orders starts out in the same way,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-197">although the sounds attached to those letters</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-198">aren&#x27;t exactly the same.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-199">When the Latin alphabet spread to other languages</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-200">in Europe and beyond,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-201">they tended to keep the same order of letters.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-202">This is a question from Quora.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-203">Why do some languages have formal</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-204">and informal versions of you, but English does not?</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-205">There&#x27;s a bit of backstory to this question.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-206">Initially, English had two second-person plural pronouns,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-207">thou and you,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-208">Thou was for addressing a singular person,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-209">you was for addressing more than one person.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-210">However, over time, because of the influence</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-211">of French in which the plural pronoun vu</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-212">can also be used as a polite pronoun,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-213">you became a respectful way</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-214">of addressing a single person as well.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-215">And at that point, thou started to fall out of use.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-216">Because if you was the respectful way</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-217">of addressing one person, then if you called someone thou,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-218">it implied that you disrespected them.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-219">So after that happened,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-220">thou eventually fell out of the language.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-221">So English was left with you</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-222">as its only second-person plural.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-223">Obviously, the problem with this</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-224">is you can no longer easily distinguish</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-225">between singular and plural.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-226">What some people have since done</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-227">is they have data-testid="transcript-caption-550">Island comes from Old English iegland.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-551">It did not have an S in Old English.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-552">But during the Middle English period,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-553">English borrowed another word meaning the same thing</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-554">from French, isle, which English now pronounces isle.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-555">The reason that isle or isle has an S in it</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-556">is that the French word</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-557">ultimately derives from the Latin word insular.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-558">So people thought, well, there&#x27;s an S in insular,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-559">therefore we should put an S in isle,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-560">even though the S was always silent</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-561">in English and in French.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-562">And once this had taken place, people thought,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-563">Wait a minute, we have these two words, isle and island.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-564">They must be related.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-565">And so they inserted a silent S</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-566">into the word island as well,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-567">even though historically</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-568">there is no reason for it to be there.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-569">MecHR asks, Why is it that some sayings</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-570">between certain languages are the same?</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-571">There could be two reasons why two languages</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-572">have very similar idioms.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-573">One could be because there are some basic metaphors</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-574">that many languages share.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-575">For example, the Spanish idiom [speaking Spanish]</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-576">means literally to throw wood on the fire.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-577">In English we would say to add fuel to the flames.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-578">But they both mean the same basic thing,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-579">which is to make a bad situation worse.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-580">The reason they could be so similar</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-581">is just that the idea that conflict or danger equals fire</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-582">is one that is found as a basic metaphor in many languages.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-583">Another reason that languages could have similar idioms</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-584">is because one language has just literally translated</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-585">an idiom from another language.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-586">A Quora user asks, Why is the word muscle</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-587">pronounced mussel?</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-588">So muscle is one of a group of words in English</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-589">where there&#x27;s a silent letter in the base word,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-590">but then that letter gets pronounced in an adjective form.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-591">Other words in this category include condemn</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-592">to condemnation and phlegm to phlegmatic.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-593">The reason for this has to do with rules</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-594">around syllables structures in English.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-595">There are certain combinations of consonants</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-596">that are not allowed to occur together</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-597">at the beginning or an end of an English syllable.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-598">So for instance, the sound sequence muscle, S-C-L,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-599">is not really permitted in English syllable structures,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-600">so instead we drop the C.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-601">However, in the word muscular,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-602">a U is added to the middle of the word</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-603">and that breaks up the syllable boundaries</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-604">so that now we have mus-cu-lar.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-605">That consonant cluster no longer exists.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-606">The word muscle comes from Latin musculus,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-607">which literally translates as little mouse.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-608">Apparently the Romans thought</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-609">that muscles look like small critters</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-610">running up and down your skin.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-611">EdLincoln6 says,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-612">Words with the same spelling and pronunciation,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-613">but different etymologies.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-614">So these would be known as homonyms,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-615">for instance bat as in the winged creature</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-616">and bat as in the stick of word.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-617">Some of these are true homonyms,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-618">as in they come from separate roots,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-619">but actually a lot of words that look like homonyms</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-620">do share a root.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-621">For example, bank as in a riverside</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-622">and bank the place where you keep your money,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-623">these actually derived from the same Germanic root,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-624">which originally meant a slope.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-625">From there, it came to mean a shoreline,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-626">the land sloping down to a river,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-627">and also a counter on which you would exchange money.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-628">ColomboSabani asks,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-629">How words to appear out of nowhere.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-632">A new word is often a blend</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-633">or a compound of two existing words,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-634">or it&#x27;s an existing word that&#x27;s changed,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-635">a noun has become a verb or an adjective has become a noun.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-636">If none of those cases apply,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-637">then an entomologist will look at other languages</p><p people will insert an R as a way</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-666">of avoiding the vowels being together,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-667">for instance in an expression like Africa and Asia.</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-668">Rdfporcazzo asks, Why is the letter R</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-669">pronounced so differently in each language?</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-670">So the letter R can be pronounced as an approximate er,</p><p data-testid="transcript-caption-671">as an alveolar trill [trills], as a uvular trill [trills],</p><p
